"Saddle querns are found in considerable numbers at Harappan sites, and they seem to have been the only means in use for grinding cereals. As their bases are usually convex, they must have been set in the earth or in mud to prevent their rocking. Materials from the Subcontinent and Distant Lands
Chanhudaro is a tiny settlement (less than 7 hectares) as compared to
Mohenjodaro (125 hectares), almost exclusively devoted to craft
production, including bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-
making and weight-making. The Harappans procured materials for craft
production in various ways. For instance, they established settlements
such as Nageshwar and Balakot in areas where shell was available. Other
such sites were Shortughai, in far-off Afghanistan, near the best source of
lapis lazuli, a blue stone that was apparently very highly valued, and Lothal
which was near sources of carnelian.
Mesopotamian texts datable to the third millennium BCE refer to copper
mining from a region called Magan, perhaps a name for Oman, and
interestingly enough, copper found at Mesopotamian sites also contains
traces of nickel. Other archaeological finds suggestive of long-distance
contacts include Harappan seals, weights, dice and beads. In this context,
it is worth noting that Mesopotamian texts mention contact with regions
named Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha, possibly the Harappan region. They
mention the products from Meluhha: carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold
and varieties of wood.
A Mesopotamian myth says of Meluhha: "May your bird be the haja-bird,
may its call be heard in the royal palace."Some archaeologists think the
haja-bird was the peacock. Did it get this name from its call? It is likely that
communication with Oman, Bahrain or Mesopotamia was by sea.
Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha as a land of seafarers. Besides, we
find depictions of ships and boats on seals.

making shell objects, including bangles, ladles and inlay?

questionText: The time span of the early Harappan phase ranges from:

options.text: 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Inverts the governing property or boundary condition.

options.text: 1900 BCE to 1300 BCE
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
For Harappan Civilization (Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology (Bricks, Beads and Bones)):
The Early Harappan phase marks the developmental stage characterized by distinct pottery, incipient craft specialization, and walled settlements (such as Kot Diji, Amri, and early Kalibangan) that preceded the mature urban planning phase (2600-1900 BCE). Chronologically, it spans from approximately 6000 BCE to 2600 BCE.

Therefore, option (C) is the correct answer.

questionText:
Read the following excerpt carefully and answer the question that follows:

"Although Harappa was the first site to be discovered, it was badly destroyed by brick-robbers. As early as 1875, Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), often called the father of Indian archaeology, noted that the amount of brick taken from the ancient site was enough to lay brick for 'about 100 miles' of the railway line between Lahore and Multan. Many of the ancient structures at the site were damaged. In contrast, Mohenjodaro was far better preserved. Cunningham, when excavating, found an ancient seal that was given to him. He tried to place it within the time-frame of the sixth century BCE to fourth century CE, the period of the earliest cities he was familiar with from Chinese pilgrim accounts, and thus missed the true antiquity of the Indus Valley."

Which pair of cities was connected by the railway track for which Harappan bricks were plundered?

detailedSolution:

Lahore and Multan
